title: Beyond ideal cavities: quantifying the impact of cavity dissipation on light-matter strong coupling
authors: Giovanna Bruno, Enrico Busani, Lorenzo Gialli, Rosario Roberto Riso, Enrico Ronca
abstract: Cavity Quantum Electrodynamics (Cavity-QED) offers a powerful framework for controlling light-matter interactions, yet first-principles approaches commonly assume ideal, lossless cavity fields. Here, we introduce a minimal extension to the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian that accounts for cavity dissipation through the experimentally accessible cavity quality factor Q. The electromagnetic field is described as a damped harmonic oscillator within the very weak damping approximation. In this framework, cavity losses only enter the light-matter interaction and dipole self-energy terms, without introducing additional photonic degrees of freedom. A time-dependent unitary transformation yields a real-valued Hermitian Hamiltonian that can be incorporated into existing ab-initio QED methods without additional computational cost or changes in scaling. We combined the approach to the QED-CCSD method and investigated the effects of cavity dissipation on the optical spectrum of a p-nitroaniline molecule under strong light-matter coupling. We found that, for realistic quality factors, cavity dissipation can reduce the Rabi splitting by more than 20% compared to the ideal-cavity limit, even though the system remains in the strong-coupling regime. Convergence towards the ideal-cavity limit then requires substantially higher quality factors than those needed to establish strong coupling. These results demonstrate that cavity dissipation can significantly affect polaritonic energetics and highlight the importance of incorporating experimentally realistic cavity losses into quantitative ab-initio Cavity-QED simulations to accurately guide experimental protocols.
summary: This theoretical work quantifies how cavity dissipation degrades the predicted energy splitting (Rabi splitting) in strongly coupled light-matter systems compared to ideal models. By modifying the Hamiltonian to account for finite cavity quality factors, the authors show that losses are a major factor, necessitating their inclusion in advanced ab-initio simulations for accurate quantum control protocols.
main_problem: The paper addresses the limitation of assuming ideal, lossless cavities in Cavity Quantum Electrodynamics (Cavity-QED) by quantifying the effect of cavity dissipation on light-matter strong coupling.
main_result: Cavity dissipation significantly reduces the Rabi splitting by over 20% for realistic quality factors, demonstrating that losses substantially modify polaritonic energetics.
method: The authors extend the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian by incorporating dissipation via a damped harmonic oscillator model, leading to a time-averaged, Hermitian Hamiltonian suitable for ab-initio QED methods.
model_or_system: The system involves light-matter interaction within a Fabry-Pérot cavity, modeled using the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian extended to include cavity damping ($\kappa = \omega_k/Q$).
important_parameters: Cavity Quality Factor (Q), coupling strength ($\lambda$), and the strong-coupling regime.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the very weak damping approximation and a first-order Maclaurin expansion of the vector potential.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the polaritonic state dispersion of p-nitroaniline in a lossy Fabry-Pérot cavity.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the modified Hamiltonian, details the mathematical transformation (PZW transformation) to maintain a real-valued, Hermitian form, and applies this framework to calculate the spectral changes using QED-CCSD.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a necessary, computationally feasible correction to standard QED models, ensuring that theoretical predictions accurately reflect experimental realities involving cavity losses.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Representation of PNA embedded in a lossy Fabry-Pérot cavity having a lifetime τ = Q/ωk, where Q is the cavity quality factor and ωk the resonance frequency of the system. The cavity axis is oriented along the z-axis, with a length inversely proportional to the resonance frequency, L ∝1/ωk, while the cavity field is polarized along the x-axis.

Figure 2: Polaritonic branches of PNA in the ideal cavity limit, Q →∞(Panel a), and for Q = 60 (Panel b). In both panels, the Rabi splitting ΩR and the corresponding cavity frequency ω are reported in eV. The time interval in panel b is set at τ = 5.01 fs corresponding to the cavity lifetime for Q = 60 and ω = 7.89 eV, which is the highest frequency considered in this analysis.

Figure 3: Convergence of the Rabi splitting towards the ideal-cavity limit as a function of the cavity quality factor Q. The deviation ∆ΩR = Ω(∞) R −Ω(Q) R is evaluated at ωc = 5.660 eV, corresponding to the minimum UP–LP separation in the ideal Q →∞limit, and at τ = 2.33 fs corresponding to the lifetime of a cavity with Q = 20 at this resonance frequency. The vertical purple dashed line marks Q = 640, above which the relative deviation falls below 1%. The horizontal black dashed line marks the corresponding threshold. The inset shows the Q = 640 −2000 range, where the deviations remain below 0.015 eV.

Figure 4: Effect of cavity dissipation on the polaritonic spectrum of PNA at the reference cavity frequency of 5.66 eV for the ideal cavity framework. (a) Evolution of the upper (UP) and lower (LP) polaritonic branches as a function of time interval τ for Q = 200. (b) Dependence of the UP and LP branches on the quality factor Q at τ = 2.33 fs which is the cavity lifetime associated with Q = 20. The color scale indicates the relative percentage deviation of the Rabi splitting from the ideal-cavity value.
